name: Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call
title: Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call
answer: This idea is about using AI to draft reading comprehension questions and to suggest guided reading groups, while keeping the teacher in charge of review and final placement. It matters because it can save teachers hours and allow more frequent checks for understanding, but group placement affects what a child reads for weeks. The teacher forms groups first, compares them with the tool's suggestion, and decides where they differ.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea addresses two time-consuming tasks in reading instruction: writing comprehension questions and forming guided reading groups. AI tools can draft comprehension questions at several levels, from simple recall to inference and analysis, and Google Forms can turn them into quick checks. The teacher reviews the questions for accuracy and removes any that could be answered without reading. A good question bank saves hours and lets teachers check understanding more often. Assessment results can also shape reading groups, but the teacher's own judgment remains the starting point.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The chapter covers kindergarten through 12th grade, and the text does not break the practice into separate grade bands. Teachers can ask AI tools to draft comprehension questions at several levels, from simple recall to inference and analysis, and can use Google Forms to turn them into quick checks. The teacher then reviews the questions for accuracy and removes any that could be answered without reading. A good question bank saves hours and lets teachers check understanding more often. For reading groups, a screener or practice platform may suggest which students belong together, but the teacher forms their own groups first, compares them with the tool's suggestion, and looks closer where the two differ.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as research on human review. It states that the research suggests a specific order: the teacher should form their own groups first, then compare them with the tool's suggestion (Krugel et al., 2023). Where the two differ, the teacher looks closer, and the teacher's judgment decides. The text does not report a study size, effect size, or other numerical finding beyond that citation.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. A tool's group suggestion is based on the data it has, so it may miss a child who tested badly on a hard day or who reads far better than they write, and the teacher knows those things. Group placement shapes what a child reads for weeks, so the decision carries weight. The teacher reviews questions for accuracy and removes any that could be answered without reading, and the teacher's judgment decides when tool suggestions differ. Using the tool as a second opinion keeps the teacher's knowledge in the decision.
